title: Most Words Made Mirrors by Swapping Letters
statement:
You get a list of lowercase words. As often as you like, you may swap any two characters, anywhere: inside one word or between two different words. Word lengths never change; only the letters move around.

Return the largest number of words that can be palindromes (read the same both ways) at the same time.

examples.why: Only e appears twice, so only one matching pair of letters exists in total, and every 2-letter palindrome needs one pair.
A 1-letter word is always a palindrome. "gg" already is one. The 5-letter word needs 2 pairs, but no other pair exists.
There are 3 pairs (a, b, g). The long word alone would eat all 3. Spending 1 pair on each short word makes 2 palindromes, like "aa" and "gg".

constraints: words[i] has only lowercase English letters
hints: Since letters can move anywhere, the original words do not matter. What resource does a palindrome of length L actually need?
A palindrome of length L needs floor(L / 2) matching pairs of letters; an odd middle can be any letter. Count how many pairs exist across all words.
Spend the pairs on the shortest words first. Sort the lengths, and take words while the pairs last.

explain.intuition:
Free swaps mean all letters go into one shared pool. A palindrome of length L is made of ⌊L / 2⌋ mirrored pairs, plus a middle letter when L is odd. The middle letters are never the problem: whatever is not used in pairs is left over, and there are always enough leftovers to fill the middles of the words you chose. So the only scarce resource is pairs.

Now it is a budget question: each word costs ⌊L / 2⌋ pairs and you want as many words as possible. Buy the cheapest first. Swapping any chosen word for a cheaper unchosen one never costs more, so the cheapest-first choice is optimal.
steps: Count every letter across all words. pairs is the sum of count[c] / 2, rounded down.
For each length L: if pairs ≥ ⌊L / 2⌋, subtract it and count the word; otherwise stop.
pitfalls: Counting words that are already palindromes. Swaps can fix others, and break these.
Worrying about middle letters. The letters not used for pairs always cover the odd middles.
Processing words in input order instead of shortest first, which can spend the pairs on one long word.

solutions.title: Check every subset
solutions.idea: A chosen set of words is achievable when the pairs it needs do not exceed the pairs available. Try every subset and keep the largest achievable one.

solutions.title: Count pairs, spend on shortest words
solutions.idea: Pairs are the only scarce resource. Sort lengths and buy the cheapest words first.

followups: Swaps are only allowed inside a single word. How does the answer change?
Each swap costs 1, and you want the most palindromes with the fewest swaps. What changes?
